articleHeadline: Where Malaria Could Return: Scientists Map the Riskiest Districts in a
articleSummary: Chongqing, China, maps malaria re-establishment risk across districts using imported cases, vectors, and habitat data. From 2014–2024, 301 imported malaria cases were recorded: Plasmodium falciparum 75.08%, P. vivax 12.29%, P. ovale 7.97% (others rare); four severe cases and three deaths. No locally acquired cases since 2011; China eliminated malaria in 2019. The vector Anopheles sinensis is widespread and pyrethroid-resistant. An ensemble niche model (biomod2) with 12 algorithms and 127 records predicts district risk; nine predictors from WorldClim/MODIS; overall AUC 0.839, TSS 0.531. Key drivers: bio5 (max monthly temp), NDVI, bio11 (mean temp). Recommendations: routine febrile screening at county hospitals, pre-departure education, and post-arrival active screening for returning workers.

articleHeadline: Simple Blood Ratio Could Flag Severe Influenza Before Treatment Begins
articleSummary: Pre-treatment neutrophil-to-platelet ratio (NPR) from routine CBCs differentiates severe from non-severe influenza in adults. articleHeadline: Monkeypox confirmed in five patients at Botkin Hospital in St. Petersburg — Fontanka
articleSummary: Five patients at Botkin Hospital in St. Petersburg have laboratory-confirmed monkeypox, with treatment ongoing and no severe illness reported. They were admitted to the hospital’s new building on Piskarevsky Prospekt. The Interregional Administration of Rospotrebnadzor is tracing contacts and has ordered disinfection. Telegram channel Mash said four patients came from one Krasnogvardeysky District apartment and interacted with a source; officials did not disclose the infection source. Monkeypox causes fever and rash, with case fatality ranging 0.1%–11% depending on strain and health. Earlier this month, at least nine people with monkeypox or suspected cases were hospitalized in Moscow region and St. Petersburg over two days, including five Zhukovsky residents on Oct 15 after contact with a possible carrier. In 2026, two tourists from Thailand and another resident had contracted monkeypox in St. Petersburg.

articleHeadline: High HIV prevalence in Eastern Region calls for urgent intervention - GAC
articleSummary: Eastern Region of Ghana has the second-highest adult HIV prevalence at 1.83% with about 42,704 people living with HIV and 1,659 new infections in 2025. Nationally, 337,435 people were living with HIV in 2025, with 13,951 new infections and 12,051 AIDS-related deaths. Women account for roughly 66% of people living with HIV, and adolescents aged 10–19 registered 1,183 new infections in 2025. District-level prevalence is led by Lower Manya Krobo at 5.08%, followed by Upper Manya Krobo (3.71%) and New Juaben South (3.02%). Among PLHIV, 70% know their status; of these, 81% receive treatment and 92% achieve viral suppression. The region calls for expanded testing, linkage to care, treatment adherence, and prevention while countering false HIV-cure claims. A regional meeting in Koforidua appointed new committee members to integrate HIV programmes into plans across 33 MMDAs.

articleHeadline: Kintampo begins clinical trial of Lassa Fever vaccine
articleSummary: Lassa fever vaccine candidate ChAdOx1 LassaJ enters Phase 1b testing at the Kintampo Health Research Centre (KHRC) in Ghana. The study enrolls 51 healthy adults aged 18–55 from Kintampo North Municipality and Kintampo South District to assess safety and immune response. Sponsored by the University of Oxford and funded by CEPI, the trial follows a prior Phase 1 study in the United Kingdom and uses the same platform as the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine. Ghana and Nigeria are endemic for Lassa fever, with Ghana reporting sporadic cases since 2011 and its largest outbreak in 2023. Recruitment is underway; participants will receive different vaccine–placebo combinations and be followed for one year. The first participant was vaccinated, marking a milestone for regional health security and KHRC’s capacity to conduct early-stage trials.

articleHeadline: Ghana Declares Yellow Fever Outbreak After Three Fatal Confirmed Cases as U.S. Travelers Need Proof of Vaccination
articleSummary: Ghana has declared a Yellow Fever outbreak in the Upper West Region after three laboratory-confirmed fatal cases. The declaration dated Oct 8 was followed by Oct 9 briefings; mass vaccination is planned in Wa West, Sissala West, and Sissala East districts for ages 9 months–60 years. U.S. travelers to Ghana must show proof of yellow fever vaccination, with entry requirements applying to travelers 9 months and older. About 450 suspected cases were reported nationwide from June–September; only lab-confirmed cases count toward the outbreak. Three deaths are confirmed; samples were confirmed at Institut Pasteur in Dakar, with later reports citing Noguchi Memorial Institute for Medical Research and other deaths under investigation. Ghana requested 187,000 additional vaccine doses; a National Rapid Response Team is deployed and isolation areas set up. Yellow fever is transmitted by Aedes and Haemagogus mosquitoes; incubation is 3–6 days; 15% of infections become severe, with high fever, jaundice and bleeding; no antiviral exists, vaccination provides lifelong protection, and travelers should seek care if fever or jaundice develops after travel.

articleHeadline: IGAD pushes for stronger animal health laboratories to boost regional disease surveillance
articleSummary: IGAD calls for strengthened animal health laboratory systems across Eastern and Southern Africa to bolster regional disease surveillance. At a Regional Training of Trainers Workshop for Laboratory Auditors on the QualiPATH Framework in Machakos, Kenya (19–23 October 2026), IGAD urged investment in competent personnel, reliable diagnostics, and harmonised standards to improve preparedness and cross-border threat detection. The five-day HEPRR-MPA-supported event gathers participants from Kenya, Mozambique, Zambia, Rwanda, DR Congo, Sao Tome and Principe, Malawi, Ethiopia and Burundi. IGAD stresses pathogens do not respect borders and highlights ongoing threats including Ebola, Marburg virus disease, Mpox, cholera, dengue and Rift Valley fever. The QualiPATH framework seeks to build a pool of competent auditors, conduct baseline assessments, mentor lab staff, and progressively reach international accreditation, reducing external dependence and strengthening national ownership. Partnerships with ASLM and ECSA-HC aim to enhance regional laboratory networks for early warning and rapid response.
